content.title: Inference Before Annotation
goals: Understand type inference and choose when an explicit annotation adds useful information.

content.question:
What type does TypeScript infer for `count`?

```ts
let count = 3;
```

feedback.correct: The initializer `3` gives TypeScript enough information to infer `number`.
feedback.incorrect: The initializer `3` gives TypeScript enough information to infer `number`.

options.text: `count` was inferred as a number, so assigning a string conflicts with that type.
TypeScript changes the variable to `string` automatically.
`count` can become any type after the first assignment.
The number `3` is ignored because the variable uses `let`.

feedback.correct: `let` means the value can change. It does not mean the variable's type becomes anything you assign later.
feedback.incorrect: `let` means the value can change. It does not mean the variable's type becomes anything you assign later.

content.title: A place where annotation helps

content.question: Which version is more useful when the type is already obvious?

feedback.correct: When the initializer already makes the type obvious, inference keeps the code cleaner without losing the type information.
feedback.incorrect: When the initializer already makes the type obvious, inference keeps the code cleaner without losing the type information.

content.title: A useful warning about `any`
content.text:
TypeScript also has a type called `any`.

`any` tells the checker to stop enforcing normal type checks for that value. That can be useful in a narrow situation, but it can also erase the very information you introduced TypeScript to preserve.

Think of it as a door marked:

**“I am choosing not to have the type checker help me here.”**

That is a deliberate decision, not a default escape hatch.

content.question: Which rule is the best default?

options.text: Annotate every variable, even when the value already makes the type obvious.
Prefer inference when the type is obvious; add annotations where they communicate a useful boundary or expectation.
Use `any` whenever a type error appears.

feedback.correct: Good TypeScript is not maximum syntax. It is useful information at the right places.
feedback.incorrect: Good TypeScript is not maximum syntax. It is useful information at the right places.

content.title: Forge takeaway & Lesson completion
takeaways: **Mental model:** Inference handles the obvious. Annotations explain the important boundaries.
**Senior habit:** Before adding a type annotation, ask, “What information does this add that the checker does not already know?”
nextSteps: Explain why this is usually enough:
and give one situation where an explicit annotation would add useful intent.
